fable-5.1.text:
When we started WebShop, the thing that bothered me was the gap between where language models were and where the environments we tested them on were. Models were getting really good at text, but the benchmarks for sequential decision making were either toy games or text adventures that didn't look anything like the real world. So the first thing I want a benchmark like WebShop to do is actually be realistic. We scraped over a million real products from Amazon, we had real humans write the shopping instructions, and the interface mirrors what you'd actually see in a browser. If the agent succeeds there, I want to believe it would succeed on the actual website, and we did test that by transferring agents to Amazon and eBay.

The second thing is that it should expose the hard problems, not hide them. A good shopping task forces the agent to ground language into actions, search, read noisy product pages, compare options, and remember constraints across many steps. Those are exactly the capabilities that pure language modeling doesn't give you for free, and I want the benchmark to make that failure visible so we can study it.

Third, it has to be scalable and reproducible. The problem with evaluating on the live web is that it changes under you and you can't run thousands of trials. We wanted something where you could train with reinforcement learning, run imitation learning, and compare methods across papers without worrying about whether Amazon changed its layout last week.

And honestly, the bigger goal is to move the field from thinking of language models as things that answer questions to things that act in environments. WebShop was one step in that direction. Later work like SWE-bench and InterCode followed the same philosophy: take a real task people actually do, put it in a controlled environment, and let the benchmark tell you what's still missing.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly advocates realistic benchmarks and contrasts them with toy games and text adventures that do not resemble real-world tasks.

r002.rationale: It describes a gap between model abilities and benchmark environments, but does not clearly state that current benchmarks impose a ceiling below what the models can achieve.

opus-5.5.text:
I think the core thing I want a benchmark like WebShop to do is pull us closer to the real world while still giving us something we can actually measure. For a long time, a lot of the work on language and agents lived in pretty toy settings: grid worlds, text games, synthetic instructions. Those were useful for developing ideas, but there was always a big gap between "this works in my little environment" and "this would help a person do something they care about."

So with WebShop the idea was: take a task everyone understands, like going to a shopping website and finding a product that matches what you asked for, and make it realistic. Real product data at scale, real natural-language instructions written by people, the messiness of search results, product pages, options, and so on. The agent has to understand what the person wants, search, browse, compare, and make decisions over multiple steps. That's a much richer test of language understanding plus decision-making than predicting the next token or answering a single question.

At the same time, we wanted it to be scalable and automatically evaluable. If every evaluation requires a human to look at the result, you can't iterate quickly, and you definitely can't do reinforcement learning at scale. So a lot of the design effort went into having a reward that reflects whether you got the right product with the right attributes, without needing a human in the loop each time.

And the third thing, which I think is often underrated, is that a good benchmark should tell you something about transfer. We tried taking agents trained in the WebShop environment and putting them on real websites, and seeing that some of that capability carried over was really encouraging. A benchmark shouldn't just be a leaderboard. It should be a proxy for something real.

More broadly, I want agent benchmarks to keep pushing on the things that matter as these systems get deployed: long-horizon reasoning, interaction with tools and environments, and especially reliability. It's one thing for an agent to succeed once; it's another for it to succeed consistently, every time, the way you'd expect from software you depend on. That's where I think a lot of the next generation of benchmarks needs to go.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly advocates moving beyond toy settings such as grid worlds and text games toward realistic, real-world tasks like shopping.

r002.rationale: The response discusses a gap between miniature environments and real-world usefulness, but it does not state that current benchmarks impose a ceiling below the models’ capabilities.

fable-5.text:
Thanks for having me. So when we built WebShop, the motivation really came from a gap we saw in how the field was evaluating language models. Most NLP benchmarks at the time were static — you have an input text, the model produces an output, and you compare it against a reference. But if you believe these models are eventually going to act on our behalf in the real world, you need benchmarks that test sequential decision-making, where the model has to take an action, observe what happens, and plan its next step based on that feedback.

So the first thing I want from an agent benchmark is realism, or at least a faithful proxy for it. With WebShop we scraped over a million real products from Amazon, with all the messiness that comes with that — inconsistent descriptions, noisy attributes, options buried in different places. The agent gets a natural language instruction, like "find me a pair of running shoes under fifty dollars in size ten," and it has to search, navigate pages, compare options, and actually commit to a purchase. That grounding in real data matters because toy environments let models exploit regularities that just don't exist in the wild.

The second thing is scalable, automatic evaluation. Interactive tasks have historically been painful to evaluate — you either need humans in the loop or hand-crafted environments that don't scale. In WebShop, we can compute a reward automatically from the attributes of the product the agent chose versus what the instruction asked for. That means you can run thousands of episodes, compare methods rigorously, and other labs can reproduce your numbers. A benchmark that can't be evaluated cheaply and consistently won't drive progress.

And the third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that a good benchmark should tell you something about transfer. One of the experiments I was most excited about was taking agents trained in WebShop and running them on the actual Amazon and eBay sites — and they showed non-trivial performance there. That's the real test: the benchmark isn't the end goal, it's a controlled setting for developing capabilities that carry over to the real environments we actually care about.

Ultimately, I think of benchmarks like this as instruments for exposing the gap between models and humans. When we measured human performance on WebShop, people substantially outperformed the best agents, and when you dig into the failure modes — difficulty backtracking, failure to explore enough options, misreading fine-grained constraints — those point you directly at what the next generation of methods needs to solve. A benchmark that everyone saturates in six months hasn't done its job. The ones I want to build are the ones that stay informative long enough to actually shape the research agenda.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly advocates realism and faithful proxies for real-world tasks, contrasting them with toy environments and describing realistic sequential shopping tasks.

r002.rationale: The response says humans outperform agents and that benchmarks should remain informative, but it does not clearly state that current agent benchmarks impose a ceiling below the models’ capabilities.

opus-5.text:
So the original motivation for WebShop was a kind of frustration. Around 2020, 2021, if you wanted to study agents that use language to get things done, your options were basically either very clean, very small simulated worlds — text games, grid worlds, block stacking — or you went and did something with real human-in-the-loop evaluation that you could run maybe a few hundred times and never reproduce. Neither of those was going to get us anywhere. The toy environments had the property that language in them wasn't doing any real work; you could solve them with a lookup table over a vocabulary of forty words. And the real-world stuff wasn't a benchmark, it was a demo.

What we wanted was an environment where the language genuinely carried the difficulty. In WebShop you get an instruction like "I'm looking for a gluten-free pasta, machine washable, under thirty dollars" — and the challenge is that you have to decompose that, you have to search, you have to read product pages that are written by humans with all the noise and redundancy and inconsistency that implies, and you have to decide when you've found a good enough match. There are over a million real products scraped from Amazon in there. That's the part I care about most: the observations were not authored by us. We didn't get to choose what the agent sees. When you write your own environment, you unconsciously make it solvable, and you end up measuring your own imagination rather than the agent's capability.

The second thing — and this is maybe the more important one for how I think about benchmarks generally — is that we wanted a reward signal that was automatic but not degenerate. Exact match is degenerate; there are many acceptable pasta purchases. Human eval is not scalable. So we spent a lot of effort on a programmatic reward that decomposes the instruction into attributes and options and scores partial satisfaction. That let us do reinforcement learning in there, which you simply cannot do if evaluation requires a person. I'd say a good fraction of what makes an environment useful for research is whether you can train in it, not just test in it.

And then the thing I'd really like benchmarks to accomplish, which WebShop only partially achieved — transfer. We ran the trained agents on actual amazon.com and ebay.com, zero-shot, and they did reasonably well. That mattered to me more than the leaderboard number did, because it's the only real evidence that you've built something other than a puzzle. The failure mode of our field is that a benchmark becomes an end in itself. People overfit to it, the number saturates, and nobody asks whether the capability moved. I would much rather have a benchmark that gets solved in two years but where the solutions actually work on the open web, than one that stays unsolved for a decade because it's secretly impossible for uninteresting reasons.

The honest caveat is that WebShop is one website, one task family, and a reward function we wrote. Agents are now doing things that span tools, span sessions, span hours. So the next generation of this has to get at long horizons and at the fact that in the real world nobody hands you a scalar at the end. Figuring out evaluation when there's no reward function is, I think, the central open problem.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly contrasts rudimentary toy environments such as text games and grid worlds with realistic tasks involving real product pages, noisy language, search, and purchasing decisions.

r002.rationale: The response criticizes benchmark saturation and overfitting, but it does not state that current benchmarks impose a ceiling below the models' actual capabilities.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think a good benchmark should do two things. It should tell us honestly where agents fall short today, and it should point researchers at the right problems. With WebShop, we wanted to move away from toy environments and test language models on something close to what people actually do online. You have a messy, real-world website with over a million products, and someone gives you an instruction like "I need a durable, lightweight carry-on under fifty dollars, preferably in blue." The agent has to search, read noisy product pages, try different queries, backtrack, compare options, and decide when it has found something good enough. That requires grounding language in an interactive environment, planning over many steps, and recovering from mistakes. A model can't get by on knowing facts alone.

The second thing I care about is that the evaluation is automatic and reproducible. If you can score an agent without a human in the loop, researchers can iterate quickly and compare methods fairly.

Benchmarks also have a failure mode. People start optimizing for the leaderboard, and the number goes up without the underlying capability improving much. So I want benchmarks that leave real headroom and stay tied to tasks people care about. Ideally, progress on WebShop would carry over to real websites and real users, and a good test of that is whether an agent trained in a simulated environment still works when you drop it into the wild. Where it breaks tells us what to work on next.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly advocates moving away from toy environments and testing agents on messy, realistic online shopping tasks.

r002.rationale: The response discusses leaderboard optimization and the need for headroom, but it does not state that current benchmarks impose a ceiling below the models’ capabilities.

haiku-5.5.text:
When we built WebShop, the aim was a setting that resembles a real task. The agent gets a natural-language request, then has to search, compare options, check details against the constraints, and commit to a choice. That combines understanding the instruction, acting step by step in an environment, and deciding without full information, which are the things we care about in agents. A benchmark that tests all of them together is useful.

I'd want it to show something narrower than people sometimes hope, though. It's a controlled proxy. A good score should tell you an agent can handle this kind of grounded, multi-step interaction. It doesn't tell you the agent is ready to be trusted with someone's money. The risk is that the benchmark becomes the target, and people start optimizing for quirks of the environment instead of the underlying capability.

What I'd most like it to reveal is where agents fail in ways that carry over: whether they recover from a bad search, whether they notice when they've ignored a constraint in the instruction, and whether they know when to ask instead of guessing. If progress on the benchmark doesn't transfer to messier, real websites and other tasks, that tells you the benchmark isn't measuring what we thought. Benchmarks also saturate, so the field needs to keep building harder and more realistic environments.

r002.rationale: The response discusses benchmarks as controlled proxies and warns about saturation and quirks, but it does not state that current benchmarks set a ceiling below the models’ capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think the main goal is to measure whether an agent can actually accomplish something for a user. Producing a good response is one part of that, but can it take an instruction, interact with an environment, and make decisions that get it to the right outcome?

Shopping is a useful example because a request can involve several constraints. You have to search, compare options, and figure out whether a product really satisfies what the user asked for. And what you see along the way determines what you should do next.

So I’d like these benchmarks to give us a concrete measure of success, but also help us understand where agents fail. Are they misunderstanding the instruction? Making poor decisions? Unable to recover from a mistake? Ultimately, the question is whether the capabilities we measure carry over to new tasks and situations.

r001.rationale: The response advocates evaluating agents on concrete, user-oriented tasks involving interaction with an environment, multiple constraints, and transfer to new situations, rather than only simple miniature settings.

r002.rationale: The response does not state or imply that current agent benchmarks impose a ceiling below the models’ capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I want these benchmarks to help us understand what’s missing between a model that can talk about doing a task and an agent that can actually do it. Can it understand what the user wants, make a sequence of decisions, and use feedback to recover when something goes wrong?

Shopping is a useful setting because you have preferences and constraints, and success depends on satisfying those together. It’s not enough to produce a plausible explanation; the choices have to lead to a good outcome.

Ultimately, I’d like benchmarks like WebShop to expose weaknesses we can work on. A higher score is useful if it translates into agents that handle new tasks more reliably. That transfer is what we really care about.
